screens.title: Core Compute Services: EC2, Lambda, ECS & Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to match an application's needs to the right AWS compute option: EC2 virtual machines, Lambda functions, or container workloads with Amazon ECS and Fargate. We'll compare control, scaling, cost model, and operational overhead so you can make architecture decisions that balance developer productivity and long-term maintenance. You'll see where full OS control matters, where event-driven serverless is more cost effective, and where containerization offers portability and microservices benefits. For each service we provide a concrete developer workflow, a common pitfall to avoid, and a practical example you could run in a prototype. By the end you will be able to justify selecting EC2, Lambda, or ECS/Fargate for a given backend component and describe the trade-offs in statefulness, resource control, and cost. Think about a mobile backend that needs image processing, REST APIs, and daily batch jobs — we'll use that scenario to show which service fits each need and why.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Developer Considerations

Developer considerations

Practical rules for deploying securely and efficiently to EC2, Lambda, and ECS/Fargate.

IAM & Security
Use IAM roles and least privilege
Assign roles to instances and tasks. Avoid embedding credentials in code or images.
Packaging
Package dependencies for runtime
Zip and upload function packages for Lambda; build reproducible Docker images for ECS/Fargate.
Networking
Secure network boundaries
Use Security Groups as virtual firewalls for EC2 and task networking for containers; avoid broad inbound rules.
Common Mistake
Using long-lived credentials instead of IAM roles or leaving ports open while debugging and forgetting to close them.
Pro Tip
Automate builds and use small base images to improve startup times and reduce attack surface.

screens.title: High-level Comparison: Control, Scaling, Cost Model
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare the three compute models across control, scaling behavior, and cost model so you can see the trade-offs clearly. EC2 gives you a virtual machine: full operating system control, the ability to select instance type, and responsibility for patching and maintenance. It scales by adding or removing instances, typically with auto scaling groups, and you pay for running instances whether they are busy or idle. Lambda removes servers: you deploy code and AWS manages compute lifecycle and scaling, so you pay only while code runs, measured in milliseconds. That makes Lambda excellent for bursty or event-driven workloads but constrains execution time and state management. ECS with the EC2 launch type is container orchestration on instances you manage; it provides container scheduling but keeps you responsible for nodes. Fargate is serverless containers: you declare C P U and memory per task and Fargate runs containers for you without managing hosts. Consider cost: EC2 can be cost-effective for steady, long-running workloads where reserved or spot pricing is used. Lambda is cost-efficient for intermittent work and small tasks. Fargate sits between: you pay for task-level resources, and you avoid node management. A common misconception is to equate serverless with no operational work — you still manage function code, permissions, and observability. Which trade-off do you expect to prioritize in your next project?

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Comparison
EC2
Full OS control
  • Resizable compute capacity as instances.
  • Manage OS, patches, and security groups.
  • Best for persistent servers and specialized hardware.
AWS Lambda
Serverless functions
  • Run code in response to events, no servers to provision.
  • Automatic scaling and pay-per-execution.
  • Good for event-driven processing and lightweight APIs.
ECS / Fargate
Containers & orchestration
  • ECS on EC2: you manage instances hosting containers.
  • Fargate: serverless containers, no host management.
  • Good for microservices and portable environments.
Scaling
EC2: add instances. Lambda: automatic per-invocation scaling. Fargate: scale tasks.
Cost model
EC2: instance-hour billing. Lambda: pay per execution time. Fargate: per-task resource billing.
Operational overhead
EC2: high. Lambda: low infra management. Fargate: medium-low.
Concrete example
An image processing worker for heavy GPU tasks is suited to EC2 GPU instances. An event-driven thumbnail generator fits Lambda. A set of microservices with shared networking and ECS task definitions maps well to ECS/Fargate.
Common misconception
Serverless eliminates all operations. In reality you still manage code, permissions, observability, and cold-start considerations.

screens.title: Amazon EC2 — Virtual Machines you control
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EC2 provides resizable compute capacity as virtual servers called instances. When you launch an instance, you control the operating system, installed packages, and runtime environment. This makes EC2 ideal for workloads that need persistent servers, custom kernel modules, or specific hardware options like GPUs. A typical EC2 workflow for a developer is to SSH into the instance, install dependencies, deploy the application, and configure security groups that act as virtual firewalls. Important developer considerations include using IAM roles for instance permissions rather than embedding credentials, automating OS patching, and monitoring instance health. Common mistakes are leaving ports open or forgetting to patch the operating system, both of which increase risk. In practice, use EC2 when you need full control over networking or the OS, or when you run long-lived processes that don't fit a function invocation model. As a reflection, if your application needs direct access to hardware or persistent disk state that you manage, EC2 is often the appropriate choice. Amazon EC2 — Virtual Machines you control means choose ec2 for full control, persistent services, and specialized hardware, while managing os maintenance and security groups.. In practical terms, resizable compute capacity and full os responsibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › EC2
Core Concept

Amazon EC2

Virtual servers you fully control, choose OS, instance type, and manage the software stack and patching.

Developer workflow
  • Launch instance with chosen AMI and instance type.
  • Use SSH to connect, install dependencies, deploy application.
  • Assign IAM role for permissions and configure Security Groups.
Common Mistake
Leaving ports open during debugging and not reverting them, or failing to patch the OS regularly.
Concrete scenario
You need a GPU-backed ML training node. Choose an EC2 instance with GPU support, install drivers and libraries, and run long-running training jobs where persistent disk and full system access are required.
Key configurations
Instance type selection (CPU, memory), security groups, IAM role, AMI and user-data for bootstrapping, and backups or snapshots for persistent storage.
Key Takeaway

EC2 is the right choice when you need full operating system control, specialized hardware, or long-running persistent services.

screens.title: EC2 Security and Operational Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Securing and operating EC2 instances requires deliberate steps you should automate where possible. Start by selecting minimal AMIs and enabling only necessary ports in Security Groups. Use Security Groups as virtual firewalls and avoid opening broad ranges to the internet. Attach an IAM role to the instance to grant permissions for AWS APIs instead of embedding credentials in code. Automate OS patching and configuration with tools such as configuration management or user-data scripts so instances are reproducible and patched. Monitor instance health and logs using centralized observability tools. Back up critical state with snapshots or managed storage so you can recover from failures. A common mistake is relying on ad-hoc manual changes: that leads to configuration drift and undetected vulnerabilities. For developers, script bootstrapping and build artifacts so deployments are repeatable. Finally, review network and IAM policies regularly to enforce least privilege. Which automation step could you add this week to reduce manual maintenance for your instances? EC2 Security and Operational Best Practices means automate patching, use iam roles, and restrict security groups to reduce risk and maintenance overhead for ec2 instances.. In practical terms, keep instances secure, patched, and properly permissioned. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › EC2 Operations
Process Flow

Secure and operate EC2 instances

A repeatable process reduces drift and exposure when managing virtual machines.

Provision
Choose minimal AMI and instance type; use user-data for bootstrap scripts.
Secure
Attach IAM role; restrict Security Groups; disable unused services.
Maintain
Automate patching, snapshots, and monitoring to detect drift and failures.
Concrete example
Create an AMI pipeline: start from a hardened base image, apply configuration, run tests, then bake a new AMI that your auto scaling group launches. This ensures consistent, tested instances.
Common Mistake
Manually logging into instances to fix issues; this leads to unreproducible changes and missing patches.
Key Takeaway

Treat instance configuration as code and automate provisioning, security, and patching.

screens.title: AWS Lambda — Serverless functions
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events without requiring you to provision or manage servers. You upload a package or container image containing your handler and dependencies, and Lambda initializes execution environments on demand. Lambda manages scaling automatically by creating additional execution environments as concurrent invocations increase. You are billed for compute time in milliseconds, which makes Lambda cost-effective for workloads that are intermittent or highly variable. A typical use case is reacting to an S3 upload: the upload triggers a function that processes the file. For developers, that means focusing on function logic and event handling instead of servers. However, there are constraints to consider: execution duration limits, potential cold-start delays when invocations occur after inactivity, and concurrency considerations that affect downstream systems. A useful misconception check: serverless means fewer servers to manage, not zero operational responsibility — you still manage code packaging, permissions, and monitoring. Consider Lambda when your workload is event-driven, stateless, and suited to short-running functions. AWS Lambda — Serverless functions means choose lambda for event-driven, stateless functions where you want automatic scaling and pay-per-execution.. In practical terms, run code in response to events without provisioning servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Lambda
Core Concept

AWS Lambda

Run code in response to events with no server provisioning. Pay only for execution time and scale automatically.

When to use
  • Event-driven jobs like reacting to S3 uploads or DynamoDB updates.
  • Short-lived stateless microservices or backend functions for mobile/web apps.
  • Automated operational tasks and real-time data processing.
Concrete example
A function triggered by S3 that resizes images, adds a watermark, and writes the result to another bucket. You pay only while the function runs and scale for bursts of uploads automatically.
Pitfall
Cold starts can add latency on the first invocation after idle periods; account for this in latency-sensitive flows.
Key Takeaway

Lambda simplifies infrastructure management for event-driven workloads, but you must plan for execution limits and cold-start behavior.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Lambda Code
Example

Python Lambda handler

A simple handler that logs an S3 event and extracts bucket and object key information for processing.

import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Lambda function to process incoming events.
    """
    print(f"Received event: {json.dumps(event)}")

    # Example: Process an S3 event
    if 'Records' in event and event['Records'][0]['eventSource'] == 'aws:s3':
        bucket_name = event['Records'][0]['s3']['bucket']['name']
        object_key = event['Records'][0]['s3']['object']['key']
        print(f"New object '{object_key}' uploaded to bucket '{bucket_name}'")
        # Add your processing logic here, e.g., image resizing, data extraction

    return {
        'statusCode': 200,
        'body': json.dumps('Function executed successfully!')
    }
Packaging & deployment
Zip the handler and dependencies or build a container image. Configure an S3 trigger and set the execution role to allow S3 read access. Keep the package small to reduce cold-start time.
Test tip
Simulate S3 event payloads during development to ensure parsing and error handling are correct before deploying.
Key Takeaway

Keep function packages minimal, grant least-privilege roles, and design for stateless execution.

screens.title: Amazon ECS & AWS Fargate — Containers for microservices
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon ECS is a managed container orchestration service for running Docker containers at scale. ECS has two launch modes: EC2 launch type, where you manage the instances that host containers, and the Fargate launch type, which is serverless for containers — you only declare C P U and memory and AWS runs the tasks. Containerization brings portability, isolation, and reproducible environments because you package your app and its dependencies together in a Dockerfile. Developers typically build images, push them to a registry such as Amazon ECR, then define Task Definitions and Services that describe how tasks run and scale. Use ECS/ECR when you want microservices with consistent environments, or when your app requires a custom runtime that doesn't fit a function. A common mistake is not optimizing Docker image size or forgetting to set resource limits in task definitions. Fargate reduces operational overhead while preserving container benefits; EC2 launch type gives more control at the cost of managing the underlying nodes. Amazon ECS & AWS Fargate — Containers for microservices means containers offer portability and consistency; fargate removes host management while ec2 launch type keeps full infrastructure control.. In practical terms, run dockerized applications with orchestration or serverless containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: ECS Launch Types: EC2 vs Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: ECS supports two launch approaches and choosing between them changes your operational responsibilities. The EC2 launch type means you provision and manage the EC2 instances that form a cluster. This gives you control over instance size, kernel configuration, and potentially lower costs if you can pack many containers onto optimized instances or use reserved/spot pricing. The trade-off is higher operational overhead: you must manage scaling, patching, and instance replacement. Fargate is serverless for containers: you specify C P U and memory per task and AWS runs container tasks without exposing hosts. Fargate reduces operational work and accelerates developer velocity because you don't provision nodes, but it can be less flexible for certain low-level optimizations. A common misconception is that Fargate always increases cost — in some cases, the reduced operational burden and better bin-packing via task sizing can offset the resource billing differences. For microservices teams that prefer minimal infra management, Fargate is often the best fit; for specialized workloads or highly optimized clusters, EC2 launch type may be preferred. screens.title: How to choose: statefulness, control, cost, and overhead
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right compute service means weighing state needs, control requirements, cost model, and acceptable operational overhead. Start with state: if your application needs persistent local state or specialized drivers, EC2 is a strong candidate. If your workload is stateless and event-driven, Lambda fits naturally. For services that benefit from container packaging and microservices architecture, ECS/Fargate provides portability and isolation. Next consider control: pick EC2 when you need kernel or OS-level customization; pick Fargate when you want to avoid managing hosts. For cost, Lambda's pay-per-execution model is cost-efficient for bursty workloads, while EC2 can be more economical for predictable, long-running workloads with reserved instances or spot optimization. Operational overhead is the final tie-breaker: choose Lambda or Fargate to reduce server management. A misconception is to base the choice on familiarity — instead, align the service to technical requirements and long-term operational expectations. Use a checklist approach: state, runtime limits, scaling model, and long-term maintenance effort to decide. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Across EC2, Lambda, and ECS/Fargate there are recurring mistakes developers make. For EC2, leaving Security Group ports open or neglecting IAM roles and system patching are common and dangerous errors. For Lambda, not accounting for cold starts or execution duration limits leads to unexpected latency or function failures when workloads exceed the model. For ECS/Fargate, oversized Docker images and missing resource limits in task definitions create slow startups and resource contention. Best practices include least-privilege IAM roles for all compute, automation of patching and image builds, and using appropriate monitoring and alerting to detect failures early. When you design with constraints in mind — such as Lambda's execution and memory limits, or ECU and network bounds on instances — you reduce surprises in production. A practical tip is to treat observability as part of your deployment: logs, tracing, and metrics help diagnose whether a performance issue is an architecture mismatch or an implementation bug. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to match an application's needs to the right AWS compute option: EC2 virtual machines, Lambda functions, or container workloads with Amazon ECS and Fargate. We'll compare control, scaling, cost model, and operational overhead so you can make architecture decisions that balance developer productivity and long-term maintenance. You'll see where full OS control matters, where event-driven serverless is more cost effective, and where containerization offers portability and microservices benefits. For each service we provide a concrete developer workflow, a common pitfall to avoid, and a practical example you could run in a prototype. By the end you will be able to justify selecting EC2, Lambda, or ECS/Fargate for a given backend component and describe the trade-offs in statefulness, resource control, and cost. Think about a mobile backend that needs image processing, REST APIs, and daily batch jobs — we'll use that scenario to show which service fits each need and why.

By the end of this chapter you will identify when to use Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda, and Amazon ECS/Fargate. You will be able to describe the fundamental characteristics and benefits of each service and explain how to choose a compute model based on requirements like statefulness, control, cost, and operational overhead. We'll focus on developer considerations such as deployment workflow, permissions, and common pitfalls so you can deploy safely and predictably. For each objective you will see a short mnemonic or visual cue that helps you remember the trade-off: control for EC2, event-driven for Lambda, and portable containers for ECS/Fargate. These skills let you justify architecture decisions, communicate trade-offs to teammates, and build a practical prototype that uses the right service for its job. Learning Objectives means match application needs to a compute service by evaluating state, control, scaling behavior, and operational overhead.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical developer tasks: how to deploy, secure, and operate each compute model. You will learn developer-centric considerations such as using IAM roles for instance permissions, packaging code and dependencies for Lambda, and building Docker images and task definitions for ECS/Fargate. We'll emphasize actionable best practices: avoid leaving ports open on security groups, prefer IAM roles over long-lived credentials, and optimize Docker images for faster startup. Each objective includes a small visual hint to aid recall: a key for IAM best practices, a package icon for function packaging, and a chip for instance tuning. These skills matter because they reduce security exposure and operational friction, and they help you deliver predictable behavior in production. By mastering these deployment steps you'll minimize common errors and focus your engineering effort on application logic rather than firefighting infrastructure issues.

Let's compare the three compute models across control, scaling behavior, and cost model so you can see the trade-offs clearly. EC2 gives you a virtual machine: full operating system control, the ability to select instance type, and responsibility for patching and maintenance. It scales by adding or removing instances, typically with auto scaling groups, and you pay for running instances whether they are busy or idle. Lambda removes servers: you deploy code and AWS manages compute lifecycle and scaling, so you pay only while code runs, measured in milliseconds. That makes Lambda excellent for bursty or event-driven workloads but constrains execution time and state management. ECS with the EC2 launch type is container orchestration on instances you manage; it provides container scheduling but keeps you responsible for nodes. Fargate is serverless containers: you declare C P U and memory per task and Fargate runs containers for you without managing hosts. Consider cost: EC2 can be cost-effective for steady, long-running workloads where reserved or spot pricing is used. Lambda is cost-efficient for intermittent work and small tasks. Fargate sits between: you pay for task-level resources, and you avoid node management. A common misconception is to equate serverless with no operational work — you still manage function code, permissions, and observability. Which trade-off do you expect to prioritize in your next project?

Amazon EC2 provides resizable compute capacity as virtual servers called instances. When you launch an instance, you control the operating system, installed packages, and runtime environment. This makes EC2 ideal for workloads that need persistent servers, custom kernel modules, or specific hardware options like GPUs. A typical EC2 workflow for a developer is to SSH into the instance, install dependencies, deploy the application, and configure security groups that act as virtual firewalls. Important developer considerations include using IAM roles for instance permissions rather than embedding credentials, automating OS patching, and monitoring instance health.
